quotes.quote: Found only in the Mekong River basin in Cambodia, around Stung Treng.

sections.html:
Betta stiktos belongs to the Betta splendens complex. IUCN Red List: Data Deficient (not enough information, but most likely highly endangered in the wild). The fish offered here are captive bred from wild-caught stock.

It is the rarest member of the Betta splendens complex. The species was once thought to be extinct, but it has reappeared in the hobby through a handful of breeders.
Found only in the Mekong River basin in Cambodia, around Stung Treng.

Native to the Mekong drainage in Stung Treng, Cambodia. It lives in swampy streams and ponds with dense vegetation and low oxygen, in still, slightly acidic water (pH 5 to 7.5) at 22 to 27°C. It uses its labyrinth organ to breathe air.

• TDS: 60 to 200 (kept in soft, low-TDS water to match wild bettas, but they tolerate a wider range)
  • pH: 5.0 to 7.0
  • Temperature: 24 to 29°C (much better coloration above 26°C)
Carnivorous. Live blackworms, frozen bloodworms and pellets are accepted.
Males are very aggressive and should be kept alone or with non-male betta tankmates. Multiple females can be kept together in a planted community tank if there is enough space.

Coloration: brown to black body with iridescent green-blue in males, with possible red patches on the fins. Females are browner with faint green. The operculum is black with a prominent, widespread snake-scale pattern of iridescent green-blue, strongest in males.

Bubblenester. The male builds a bubble nest under a floating leaf or plants and places the eggs in it after spawning. Remove the female once spawning is done. Eggs hatch in 24 to 48 hours, and the fry are free-swimming about 3 days later. Start them on infusoria, then move to baby brine shrimp. Keep the surface calm so the nest stays intact.

Stiktos look similar to smaragdina but have a smaller, stouter body, shorter fins, and a spotted dorsal fin. Their snake-scale pattern is less spread across the body and more prominent on the face and gill plates.

  • Body: compact and slender with a stout head; smaller than most splendens-complex relatives, reaching about 2.8 cm standard length (maximum size 5 cm).
  • Tail: exclusively roundtail, with short caudal and anal fins. Up to 9 rows of black transverse bars on the caudal fin and 5 rows of round black spots on the dorsal fin, which give the species its "spotted" look.
